query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount (~0.1 at.%) of boron into a dual‐phase Ti40Zr40W10Mo10 refractory high-entropy alloy will trigger intergranular boride precipitation that reinforces grain boundary cohesion, thereby enhancing ductility and uniform deformability during dynamic loading without diminishing the matrix strength or slowing the fast, impact‐induced energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: Dual‐phase Ti40Zr40W10Mo10 alloy with a BCC matrix interspersed with Mo-W-rich precipitates that enable high compressive strength and considerable impact energy release but have limited uniform deformability.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor boron doping (~0.1 at.%) during alloy synthesis to promote the precipitation of fine, intergranular borides.
generation.conditions: Ambient temperature and high strain-rate (e.g., 3000 s⁻¹) dynamic compression tests simulating impact conditions typical for energetic structural materials; standard processing and heat-treatment protocols used for the baseline alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine intergranular HCP-type borides at the grain boundaries
generation.mechanism: The boron-induced precipitates enhance grain boundary cohesion, shifting the failure mode from predominantly intergranular to transgranular, which increases both ductility and work hardenability. Because the precipitation is localized at the boundaries, the high-strength dual-phase matrix responsible for rapid reaction and energy release under impact remains largely unchanged.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the untreated Ti40Zr40W10Mo10 alloy, the boron-doped variant will exhibit a noticeable increase in fracture strain (i.e. improved ductility and more uniform plastic deformation) under dynamic loading conditions, while maintaining similar dynamic compressive strength and energy-release characteristics (e.g., reaction speed and violence).
generation.baseline: The undoped Ti40Zr40W10Mo10 high-entropy alloy, which already displays high strength and a pronounced energy-release mechanism under impact but suffers from relatively lower ductility and non-uniform deformability.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only at low boron levels (~0.1 at.%); higher boron contents may lead to excessive secondary phase formation that could degrade overall strength or interfere with energy release. The effect is anticipated to hold under high strain-rate impact conditions and may need revalidation at elevated temperatures or in alternative dual-phase HEA compositions.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends the results from PMC9572892 (which demonstrated that minor boron addition in a HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy improves ductility by promoting intergranular boride precipitation) and PMC11767206 (which established that the dual-phase Ti40Zr40W10Mo10 alloy attains high strength and energy release). It is new in that it combines intergranular strengthening via boron with a dual-phase energetic alloy architecture to target the simultaneous optimization of ductility and energy release – an area not directly explored in the current literature.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ti40Zr40W10Mo10 samples by identical melting and thermo-mechanical processing routes – one set with ~0.1 at.% boron doping and one set as the control. Subject both sets to dynamic compression tests at a high strain rate (e.g., 3000 s⁻¹) to simulate impact, complemented by high-speed imaging to capture energy-release events. Microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM) will assess the grain boundary precipitates and fracture modes.
measurements: Dynamic compressive yield strength and ultimate strength
High-speed imaging data quantifying reaction delay and intensity of energy release
Microstructural analysis of grain boundaries (presence, size, and distribution of boride precipitates)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in ductility/uniform deformability (i.e., fracture strain) under dynamic loading relative to the control, or if the dynamic compressive strength or energy-release characteristics are substantially degraded (e.g., reaction intensity reduced or delays increased), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study demonstrates that the addition of W significantly enhances the mechanical properties of TiZrMo alloys, with the phase ratio effectively being controlled by adjusting the elemental composition. As a result, a dual-phase Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA was successfully fabricated and subjected to comprehensive quasi-static and dynamic loading experiments to evaluate its energy release capability and mechanical properties for potential structural applications. The Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA demonstrated exceptional quasi-static mechanical performance, with a yield strength of 1490 MPa, an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa, and a fracture strain of 30%. Under dynamic loading at a strain rate of 3000 s−1, the alloy exhibited an even higher ultimate strength of 2300 MPa and maintained a fracture strain of 24%, showcasing its remarkable ability to retain plasticity under extreme conditions. Additionally, the Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA displayed significant chemical energy release and a high energy release capacity. Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.

Dai’s team analyzed the energy-release process and overpressure of two types of high-entropy alloy fragments, WFeNiMo [] and FeNiCoCr [], in the velocity range, of 500–1800 m/s. It was shown that compared with tungsten alloy, WFeNiMo high-entropy alloy has better energy-releasing characteristics. Ren [] analyzed the mechanism of compression and energy release of TiZrNbV alloy by numerical simulation and experiments. However, the energy-release threshold of the existing high-entropy-alloy energetic-structure materials is relatively high, regardless of whether it is measured by strain rate or impact velocity. Furthermore, chemically active rare-earth elements have not been doped into high-entropy alloys as energetic structural materials. As a rare-earth element, cerium is chemically active. To balance the trade-off between mechanical properties and energetic characteristics, we introduced cerium into the Al0.5NbZrTi1.5Ta0.8 matrix and investigated the effect of cerium content on the dynamic compressive mechanical properties and energy-releasing characteristics of Al0.5NbZrTi1.5Ta0.8Cex high-entropy alloy.
